sm: Michael Knowles joins the hosts for a Thanksgiving week conversation about the holiday's history and his own family ties to it. He explains that his cigar company is named for the Mayflower because his father's side descends from it. He describes the passengers as misfits as much as aristocrats, split between religious separatists and so-called strangers. His ancestors include Dr. Samuel Fuller, John Billington, who was the first man executed for murder in Plymouth, and Stephen Hopkins, whose shipwreck and mutiny inspired Shakespeare's Tempest. The hosts then read out their own Mayflower ancestors and joke that they may be distant cousins.

The group turns to the courage of the voyage and the tension between passengers and crew. The ship was blown far off course to Cape Cod, where the settlers found abandoned camps and stored corn. Two Native men, Samoset and Squanto, walked out of the woods speaking English. Knowles recounts Squanto's story of capture, slavery in Spain, and time in England, and says the Pilgrims saw it as divine providence. He rejects both the cheerful civic myth and the revisionist version. He argues that Massasoit and Squanto were shrewd political actors, that Edward Winslow's broth helped save Massasoit, and that the alliance lasted until King Philip's war. He says the revisionism strips Native Americans of agency and that the early settlers deserve gratitude.

Asked about Plymouth's early experiment with shared property, Knowles says Governor Bradford recorded that when everyone owns everything, people stop working and starve. Within about a year Bradford assigned private parcels of land and required people to work for their food. Knowles tells the story of Bradford confiscating children's toys on Christmas Day because the separatists rejected the holiday. The hosts note that even with an unusually unified community, people began slacking within weeks. They also discuss the Roanoke colony, which they say was likely absorbed by a nearby Native community, and joke about cannibalism.

The conversation moves to modern Thanksgiving. Knowles likes formality, hosts a traditional dinner with turkey rather than prime rib, and skips football. He notes the first Thanksgiving featured venison and perhaps lobster, and that the Puritans abolished feast days yet created one that Americans still keep. He talks about being the conservative uncle at the family table and his viral skits on the subject. To close, he says telling the Mayflower story matters because patriotism is a starting point, like love of one's parents, and that a country disappears when its stories and rituals stop being passed on.
